explanation: Fires on noun/adjective tokens inside technical (mostly biomedical, sometimes engineering) phrases about a quantity, dose or rate that is increased, reduced or high, e.g. 'high[ tidal] volumes', 'lethal dose', 'reduces infar[ct] size', 'associated with [high] morbidity', 'reduces the [data] size'. The token itself varies; what matters is the context of a measured amount being raised, lowered or extreme. Function words like 'the' after 'increase'/'reducing' also fire. Everyday text fires weakly.

Fires most on the first token of a code body right after the import/namespace/header block: 'public' after Java imports or a Javadoc, '{' after a C# namespace line. Weaker unrelated hits include 'and [so] on', 'third [derivative]' in math problems, license boilerplate ('free [software]', 'use [in] source'), and assorted code punctuation.

Fires on words about mixing or combining things, like 'mixed', 'mix', 'mixture', 'stream [of] mixed fuel', 'liquid-solid', 'stirring'. It also fires on the article or preposition just before a mixture is named ('a [a] mixture of', 'a mobile phase consisting of [a]'). Fires strongest when the context is physical or chemical mixing; figurative uses ('mixed evidence', 'a mix of') are moderate.

A diffuse unit with no clear shared concept. It fires on function words in the middle of a clause (same, than, just, without, not, until, after, 'we', 'they') across general web text, and on '=' or a blank operand in algebra word problems ('Solve 18 [=] -3*y'). The marked token is usually a short word that continues the clause, but there is no single theme.

Fires on a word-initial subword fragment of a proper noun or rare word that has been split into pieces, especially 'ag'/'Mag'/'Ag' (Sagittarii, MagickWand, Magdalen, Agence, magrittr, magento). Also fires on similar fragments such as 'Tri', 'Aug', 'Austral', 'Tab' and 'ac'. What matters is the token being the first piece of a longer word. Ordinary whole words fire weakly.

No coherent pattern. Top hits include 'construction' (machinery, workers, sites), shell command flags ('-q', '-la'), jQuery/Angular '$.' and '.$', LaTeX '$', Chinese commas, format '%' signs, and assorted prose words. It looks like a mixture of the construction-industry concept and code/shell punctuation tokens.

Fires on tokens that express variation, difference or interaction within and between groups, like 'Intra-[ and] inter-', 'within [and] between', 'inter-', 'diversity between', 'tensions between', 'sectarian violence', 'factionalism', 'schism', 'gene flow'. The strongest hit is 'and' in the 'intra- and inter-' construction. Some weak, unrelated code hits occur.

A mixture. It fires on 'the [safety] (and efficacy) of' in clinical abstracts, on 'a [number] of' and '[mechanism(s)]', on 'horizontal'/'horizont', on oxygen/superoxide, and on an SVG path 'v' command, plus scattered other nouns. The common thread is a fairly abstract head noun after 'the'/'a' in a scientific or technical sentence, but the hits do not share one theme.

Fires on the head word of a compound or category name right after a modifier that marks its domain: 'golf [course]', 'German [automobile] club', 'sports[-car]', 'public [golf] course', 'Bombers [Football] Club', 'Unix-like', 'Simplify [(]'. It also fires on the opening bracket of math/regex expressions. Mixed in are scattered Russian words and noun hits like 'ability'. No single clean concept.

Fires on the second part of a fixed multi-token unit, completing a set expression or name: '2 1[/]2', '6 1/[2]', 'one-and-a[-half]', 'period[ont]al', 'Street [Fighter]', 'Wizard of [Oz]', 'Use of this [source] code', 'menos [que]', 'enter[ic]'. The prediction is that it fires where the next token is nearly determined by the preceding fragment. Fractions and 'half' are the clearest cases.

Fires on hard-to-predict subword pieces inside rare names, codes and abbreviations: random ID strings ('ih4GNX...[d]'), Latin taxon fragments ('C[erc]opithecidae', 'Emperor [p]enguins', 'Maine Co[on]'), legal case formatting ('[v].', 'County Court at [Law]'), and acronym letters. It also fires on '=o' in math. It responds to the middle of unusual tokenized strings, not to ordinary words.

Fires mainly on tokens in Russian text that appears mixed in with code or technical content (prepositions such as 'к', 'в', 'на', and words like 'наши', 'несколько'). It also fires on shell flags ('-type', '-o') next to French or Russian comments, on digits in copyright years, and on 'mis-' prefixes. The core job is non-English (mostly Cyrillic) prose in programming contexts, with unrelated extras.

Fires on tag-question and confirmation-seeking tokens at the end of a statement: 'isn['t] it?', 'aren't one of us, [are] you?', ', [right]?', 'haven['t]', 'don['t] you think'. It is strongest on the tag itself just before '?'. 'right' in other senses ('right now', 'right here', 'right back') fires only moderately, and commas fire weakly.

Fires on tokens inside software packaging, build and license boilerplate: Homebrew cask fields, NetBSD '$NetBSD: ...,v' headers, 'included in the packaging of [this] file', 'main directory of [this] source tree', autoconf 'AC_'/'ac_', version suffixes ('-p385', '-mingw32'), and Unix paths ('/etc', '/usr/c'). The context of a config, packaging or license file matters more than the token itself.
